claims.text: Resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in oxide-forming HEAs is governed by adaptive passivation.
A protective oxide or spinel film rapidly regenerates after being mechanically removed.
Adaptive film regeneration can make combined degradation lower than the sum of isolated wear and corrosion.
The proposed initial HEA has a homogeneous, single-phase solid-solution microstructure.
A homogeneous single-phase HEA can be predisposed to form a passivating oxide film in situ.
Cr or Mn can serve as the critical oxide-forming additions responsible for rapid passivation in the proposed comparison.
The relevant structural mediator is a protective surface oxide or spinel film.
Mechanical wear intermittently removes the protective oxide film during combined exposure.
Available oxide-forming elements accelerate re-formation of the worn film.
Rapid film re-formation limits damage by preventing continuous alloy exposure to the corrosive medium.
An HEA lacking the critical oxide-forming elements will show combined degradation close to the additive effects of isolated wear and corrosion.
The oxide-forming HEA will have lower total degradation under simultaneous wear and corrosion than the matched baseline.
The oxide-forming HEA will exhibit combined degradation below the sum of its isolated wear and corrosion components.
The prediction should hold when the mechanical film-removal rate does not exceed the film-regeneration rate.
The prediction should hold only under environmental conditions that support oxide-film formation.
Aggressive wear or inhibition of oxide formation will cause the adaptive-passivation mechanism to fail.
